```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
engines <- all(vapply(c("duckdb", "DBI", "arrow", "nanoarrow"), requireNamespace, TRUE, quietly = TRUE))
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(zuint)
```

## The four types

zuint has one type for each wide integer type that Arrow and DuckDB use.
Each type gives up one bit pattern to `NA`, so its range is one value short
of the full width.

| zuint | Arrow | DuckDB | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int64` | `int64` | `BIGINT` | ±(2^63^ − 1) |
| `uint64` | `uint64` | `UBIGINT` | 0 to 2^64^ − 2 |
| `int128` | `arrow.opaque` hugeint | `HUGEINT` | ±(2^127^ − 1) |
| `uint128` | `arrow.opaque` uhugeint | `UHUGEINT` | 0 to 2^128^ − 2 |

The constructors convert from numbers, strings and each other. A conversion
is exact, or it gives `NA` with a warning:

```{r}
uint64("18446744073709551614")
int128("-0x7fff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff")
int64(c(2^53, 1.5))
```

`int64` keeps the storage of bit64's `integer64` and has it as its second
class, so packages that read `integer64` read `int64` unchanged.

## Mixing types

When two types meet, the result is the smallest type that holds both, so no
value is lost. `int128` and `uint128` hold different values, so they have no
common type, and mixing them is an error.

```{r}
zu_common_type(int64(1), uint64(1))
int64(-1) + uint64("18446744073709551614")
try(int128(1) + uint128(1))
```

A double takes the zuint type if it is a whole number in range, and is an
error otherwise; comparisons with doubles are exact and never an error:

```{r}
int64(10) + 2
try(int64(10) + 0.5)
int64("9007199254740993") > 2^53
```

## Overflow policies

The operators give `NA` with a warning when a result is out of range, as R's
integers do. The `checked_*()` functions make it an error, and the
`wrapping_*()` functions compute modulo 2^64^ or 2^128^:

```{r}
big <- int64("9223372036854775807")
big + 1L
try(checked_add(big, 1L))
wrapping_mul(uint64("0xffffffff"), uint64("0xffffffff"))
```

`sum()` keeps the type and is exact, or `NA` with a warning; `mean()` and
`median()` are doubles computed from the exact values:

```{r}
x <- int128(c("170141183460469231731687303715884105727", "1", "-1"))
sum(x)
mean(int64(1:2))
```

## Through engines and back

```{r, include = !engines, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("*The examples in this section need the duckdb, DBI, arrow and nanoarrow packages, which are not installed here.*")
```

`zu_duckdb_query()` reads a query's wide integer columns exactly, and
`zu_duckdb_register()` hands a data frame back to DuckDB with their types:

```{r, eval = engines}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
df <- zu_duckdb_query(con, "
  SELECT 18446744073709551614::UBIGINT AS id,
         -170141183460469231731687303715884105727::HUGEINT AS total
")
df
zu_duckdb_register(con, "back", df)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT typeof(id) AS id, typeof(total) AS total FROM back")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

The same columns go through Arrow tables, and so through Parquet files:

```{r, eval = engines}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(zu_arrow_table(df), f)
zu_from_arrow_table(arrow::read_parquet(f, as_data_frame = FALSE))
```

Underneath, `zu_to_arrow()` and `zu_from_arrow()` speak the Arrow C Data
Interface directly, and `nanoarrow::convert_array(array, int64())` uses them
when nanoarrow is installed.

## Where the class gets lost

Base functions that build their result from the bare values read the raw
bits as numbers. The ones you meet first:

* `c(1L, x)` and `sum(2L, x)` dispatch on their first argument, so with a
  base number first they never reach zuint: put the zuint vector first.
* `sapply()`, `unlist()` and `tapply()` drop the class of what they
  collect: use `zu_vapply()`, or `do.call(c, list)`.
* `ifelse()` builds its answer from `yes` and `no` without their class.

`zu_ifelse()` and `zu_vapply()` keep the type:

```{r}
x <- int64(c("-9223372036854775807", "5"))
zu_ifelse(x > 0L, x, int64(0))
```

For the same reason, `serialize(ascii = TRUE)` and `dput()` do not keep the
values of negative `int64` numbers or of `NA`; R's default binary
serialization does.
